passage:
In the kitchen of the shared house in Johannesburg, Thabo laid the receipts on the table. It was the fourth time that Lucia, Thabo's partner of three years, had said she was at work when she was not. Each time there had been a new explanation, and each time Thabo had believed it.
"I don't know what is true anymore," Thabo said quietly. The anger was there, but underneath was grief, and a small voice asking whether Thabo had been foolish.
Lucia said, "It's not what you think," again.
"I can't keep doing this. Until things are honest, I need space. I'm going to my brother's. I am also booking time with a counsellor."
Thabo picked up the keys.

qa.q: How many times had Lucia said she was at work when she was not?
qa.a: It was the fourth time Lucia had said she was at work when she was not.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling while laying the receipts on the table?
qa.a: Thabo felt angry, grieving and doubtful of the self. The quiet "I don't know what is true anymore" shows the loss of trust.

qa.q: What boundary and support did Thabo choose?
qa.a: Thabo said space was needed until things were honest, went to a brother's place and planned to see a counsellor. That protected trust and helped Thabo regain clarity.

qa.q: What might Lucia have been feeling when repeating "It's not what you think"?
qa.a: Lucia may have felt cornered and afraid of losing Thabo, yet the repeated line gave no real answer. Thabo had heard it before, so it could not rebuild trust.

grounding: A person finding repeated lies from a partner feels anger, self-doubt and grief, and sets a boundary and seeks a counsellor.

The community centre's counselling room had a small plant and a box of tissues. Irawati sat down and twisted the strap of her bag.
"Ankita, my brother told me again that he repaid the loan money to our mother. It is the fifth time he has said something and it turned out false. I feel stupid. I keep thinking I should have known."
The counsellor, Ankita, said gently, "It sounds like you are angry and also grieving someone you thought you knew. It's not stupid to trust family."
They talked about what Irawati could say: "I love you, but until I see it myself, I won't lend or vouch for anything." Irawati wrote it on a card and slid it into her bag.

qa.q: How many times had Irawati's brother said something false?
qa.a: It was the fifth time he had said something that turned out false.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling as she twisted the strap of her bag?
qa.a: Irawati felt anxious, foolish and angry, and was grieving the trust lost. The twisting strap shows how heavy it felt.

qa.q: What did Ankita help Irawati do?
qa.a: Ankita named the anger and grief, said it is not stupid to trust family and helped Irawati write a clear boundary on a card. That gave Irawati something concrete to say.

qa.q: How might Irawati's brother see the boundary on the card?
qa.a: Her brother might feel hurt or defensive at first, but it states love and a clear limit. Repeated false statements had used up the trust.

grounding: A person finding repeated lies from a family member feels anger, self-doubt and grief, and a counsellor helps set a boundary.

passage:
Pema found out on a Tuesday, in their Delhi flat, that Jagdish had not told his parents about their engagement. For the third time. He had said, in March, "I told them, they're fine." In June: "They're coming around." Today his mother had called Pema by mistake and asked, puzzled, who she was.
Pema sat on the balcony for an hour. She felt furious, then foolish, then very sad. How had she believed him three times? Was she stupid? Was anything he said true?
That night she called her oldest friend, Chhoki, and talked until two. Chhoki said, "You're not stupid. You trusted him. That's different."
The next day Pema told Jagdish calmly, "No more stories. We go to your parents together this month, or I step back from the engagement. And I've booked a counsellor. I want to go, with or without you."
Jagdish, grey-faced, said, "With."

qa.q: Who called Pema by mistake?
qa.a: Jagdish's mother had called Pema by mistake.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling on the balcony?
qa.a: Pema felt furious, then foolish, then very sad, and began doubting herself for believing him three times.

qa.q: Which steps helped Pema regain clarity?
qa.a: Talking with a trusted friend, setting a clear boundary with a consequence, and booking a counsellor for support.

qa.q: How did Jagdish react to Pema's boundary?
qa.a: Jagdish looked grey-faced and shaken, and chose to go to the counsellor with her.

grounding: A person finding a partner's repeated lies feels anger, self-doubt and grief, then sets a boundary and seeks a counsellor and friend.

"Mehak, sit. I know you haven't been going to college."
"Vikas Bhaiya, I—"
"Please let me finish. In January you said the classes were online. In March you said exams were postponed. Last week you said you had a holiday. None of it was true. I checked."
"I was going to tell you."
"You've said that too. Three times."
"...I know."
"I've been so angry I couldn't sleep. And then I started thinking, maybe I'm the fool for believing you. I talked to Anand about it for hours. He helped me see it clearly."
"I'm sorry, Bhaiya. I just couldn't tell Papa I'd dropped out."
"Here's what happens now. I won't lie to Papa for you anymore. Sunday, we tell him together. I'll sit next to you. After that, you and I see the college counsellor about what's next."
"And if I don't?"
"Then I tell him myself. I'm done covering."

qa.q: When does Vikas plan to tell Papa together with Mehak?
qa.a: Sunday, they tell him together.

qa.q: What had Vikas been feeling since finding out about the lies?
qa.a: Vikas was so angry he couldn't sleep, and then began doubting himself, wondering if he was a fool for believing Mehak.

qa.q: Which of Vikas's choices protect trust going forward?
qa.a: He set a clear boundary that he won't lie for Mehak anymore, a firm consequence if Mehak refuses, and a plan to see the college counsellor together.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel hearing the boundary?
qa.a: Mehak likely feels ashamed and scared, but also relieved not to face Papa alone.

grounding: A brother who finds repeated lies feels anger and self-doubt, talks to a friend, and sets a clear boundary with consequences.

passage:
I'm Jahnavi, and the year Joseph and I were together, he lied to me about where he was, again and again. "Late meeting." "Stuck at my cousin's." "Phone died." Small things, each one. I found out about the first one by accident, forgave it, then found another. By the fifth, I didn't know which of his words were real.
The worst part wasn't the anger, though I was angry, so angry my hands shook. It was the grief, for the person I thought he was. And the doubt, for myself. Was I too trusting? Too needy?
A friend gave me the number of a counsellor. Those sessions helped me untangle it: his lies were his choice, not my failure.
I told Joseph clearly: one more lie and I'm leaving. He lied again two weeks later.
I left. It hurt. But I trusted myself again.

qa.q: How many lies had Jahnavi found by the time the doubt set in?
qa.a: By the fifth, Jahnavi didn't know which of his words were real.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling beyond anger?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt grief for the person Joseph seemed to be, and doubt about whether being too trusting was the problem.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi regain clarity and stay protected?
qa.a: Seeing a counsellor to understand the lies were Joseph's choice, then setting a clear boundary and following through.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen the boundary before he lied again?
qa.a: Joseph may not have believed it was real, perhaps expecting to be forgiven again, as Jahnavi had forgiven the first lie.

grounding: A person facing a partner's repeated lies feels anger, grief and self-doubt, seeks a counsellor and holds a boundary.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage: Counselling note, Thursday, 5 p.m. Aadhya, 25, came in holding a printout: the college portal showing her brother Arnab had not attended a single MBA class since March. He had told her every week that classes were "fine, tiring". When she asked last month, he lied again, then twice more. Today she swung between anger ("He looked me in the eye") and self-doubt ("How did I not see it? Am I stupid?"), then cried quietly about "the brother I thought I had". I told her that people who trust are not stupid; they are trusting. We worked on two boundaries she can keep: she will stop covering for Arnab with their parents, and she will not discuss his fees until he tells them himself. She wrote both in her own words. She plans to talk it through with her cousin Riddhi, whom she trusts, before speaking to Arnab on Sunday. Follow-up booked for next Thursday.

qa.q: Since when had Arnab not attended a single MBA class?
qa.a: Since March.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she asked "Am I stupid?"
qa.a: Aadhya felt self-doubt and shame, wondering how she had missed the lies, alongside anger at being deceived.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor help Aadhya take?
qa.a: Naming two boundaries in her own words, no covering and no talk of fees until he tells their parents, and talking to Riddhi, a cousin she trusts, before facing Arnab.

qa.q: What would change if Aadhya kept covering for Arnab with their parents?
qa.a: The lies would stay easy for Arnab and the weight would stay on Aadhya, so trust would keep wearing down with nothing changing.

grounding: Shows a young woman hurt by her brother's repeated lies, feeling anger, self-doubt and grief, and setting boundaries with a counsellor's help and a trusted cousin's support.
